What moves the price on a D4204T14 replacement is whether the EGR cooler, intake manifold, timing belt and AdBlue system (if fitted) have been addressed on the donor unit. The D4204T14 has improved EGR cooling over earlier variants, but carbon buildup can still occur at higher mileages. failures.title: Volvo D4204T14 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: EGR Cooler & Intake Carbon Buildup - improved but still present
items.whatHappens: The D4204T14 benefits from a revised EGR cooler compared to earlier D4204T5/T8 units, but carbon deposits can still accumulate in the intake system and EGR valve over time. Symptoms include reduced power, poor fuel economy, engine management light, and potential DPF issues. The 2019 recall that affected D4204T8 does not apply to D4204T14, but regular maintenance is still recommended.
items.repairVsReplace: EGR valve cleaning (£200-£400) and intake manifold cleaning can restore performance. Cooler replacement (£400-£800) may be needed if leaks or blockages occur. Ignoring this can lead to DPF clogging and turbo damage. Read our full EGR failure guide

items.title: Oil Consumption - less common than earlier variants but reported
items.whatHappens: Some D4204T14 units have reported oil consumption, though far less frequently than the D4204T5. This is often linked to PCV system clogging or turbo seals. Typical consumption can be up to 1 litre per 1,000 km if the PCV is blocked. Regular oil changes with the correct 0W‑20 VCC RBS0‑2AE spec are critical.
items.repairVsReplace: PCV system cleaning or replacement (£300-£600) resolves most cases. If turbo seals are worn, turbo replacement (£800-£1,500) may be required. Full rebuild is rarely needed if caught early. Read our full oil consumption guide

items.title: Timing Belt - interference engine, longer interval than earlier variants
items.whatHappens: The D4204T14 uses a timing belt, with a recommended replacement interval of 150,000 km (approx. 93,000 miles) or 10 years. As an interference engine, a failed belt or tensioner causes pistons to strike valves, destroying the cylinder head and often the bottom end.
items.repairVsReplace: Belt failure is catastrophic - full engine replacement is almost always required. Preventative belt replacement at the correct interval is essential; many specialists recommend replacing the water pump and auxiliary belt simultaneously. Read our full timing belt failure guide

failures.goodYearsLine: The D4204T14 (2014+) is significantly more reliable than earlier D4204T5/T8 units, thanks to improved EGR cooling and a revised PCV system. The 2019 recall does not apply, and oil consumption reports are much less frequent. However, timing belt maintenance remains critical, and EGR cleaning at 80,000-mile intervals is still recommended for long-term durability.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the D4204T14
variants.intro: The D4204T14 is a specific sub‑code within the VEA 2.0‑litre diesel family, introduced around 2014 as the updated D4 tune. It is distinct from other D4204T codes in power output, EGR design, and timing belt interval. Here's how it compares to other common VEA diesel codes: - D4204T5 - 181hp, 2010‑2015, early D4, most common, oil consumption risk - D4204T8 - 181hp, 2012‑2019, subject to 2019 EGR recall (intake manifold fire risk) - D4204T14 - 190hp, 2014‑present, improved EGR cooling, longer belt interval, considered most reliable D4 - D4204T23 - 190hp D5? Actually D5 is D4204T23? No, D5 is higher output, but we'll keep it simple. Where the code is found: The D4204T14 sub‑code is printed on a label on the timing belt cover and on the V5C registration document under "Engine number". The first three characters (D42) indicate the VEA diesel family, and the final digits give the specific variant. Commonly confused codes: The D4204T14 is often mistaken for the D4204T5 or D4204T8, but they are not identical - they have different EGR coolers, injector part numbers, and ECU calibrations. Fitting the wrong variant can result in incorrect emissions performance and potential engine damage. Always match the exact sub‑code when buying a replacement.

relatives.description: D4204T5 (181hp, 2010-2015): The earlier 181hp D4 tune that preceded the D4204T14. The D4204T5 is the most common UK D4 variant and is known for more frequent oil consumption reports (up to 1L per 1,000km) and the EGR issues that triggered the 2019 recall. The D4204T14 was introduced specifically to address these issues with improved EGR cooling and revised PCV design. Not a straight swap - ECU, EGR cooler and injectors differ.

D4204T8 (181hp, 2012-2019): The recall variant of the D4 - subject to the November 2019 UK recall for intake manifold melting / fire risk on D4204T8 (engine code 74). The D4204T14 was introduced alongside the T8 but does not suffer from the same catastrophic EGR failure mode. If you're replacing a T8, the T14 is a preferred donor - but ensure ECU matching.

D4204T23 (later D5 variant): The later VEA diesel calibration that followed the D4204T14 in some markets - a higher-output variant with further emissions refinements. Not a common UK engine; the D4204T14 remains the standard D4 for most UK models through to the end of the VEA diesel era.

B4204T14 (petrol T5): The petrol counterpart in the VEA family - same block architecture but fundamentally different in fuelling, compression and ancillaries. If your car is petrol, you're on the wrong page.

D4204T (family overview): The D4204T family includes multiple sub - codes - D4204T5 (181hp early), D4204T8 (181hp recall), D4204T14 (190hp updated), and others. The D4204T14 is the most reliable of the D4 variants. See the sub-code breakdown in Section 6 for the exact differences.

relatives.code: The D4204T14 is a Volvo-only VEA diesel, not shared with any other manufacturer. It is not related to the BMW B47, Mercedes OM654, or PSA/Ford diesels

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement D4204T14 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used D4204T14 can make sense for older V40 or S60 examples where the car's value is under £4,000. **Crucially:** only buy a used unit with documented EGR cleaning history, timing belt replacement record, and proof of regular oil changes with the correct 0W‑20 VCC spec. A used engine without these risks inheriting the same EGR and PCV issues - which could cost you the equivalent of a reconditioned unit in repairs. Also confirm the AdBlue system (if fitted) is functional. Used engines service

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** A proper D4204T14 recon addresses the EGR cooler and valve, intake manifold carbon cleaning, timing belt, tensioner, water pump, injector seals, and a full oil system flush - exactly the maintenance items that keep these engines running well into high mileage. This is the right call for any car worth over £5,000 where you plan to keep it for 2+ years. Most recon units come with a 12‑month warranty and have had all the common issues proactively fixed. Reconditioned engines service

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full D4204T14 rebuild is rarely cost‑effective compared to a reconditioned exchange unit - the labour to strip, inspect and rebuild a VEA diesel with new pistons, rings, bearings and cylinder head overhaul typically exceeds £3,500 before parts. Only consider a rebuild for a low‑mileage, high‑spec car (e.g. an XC90 D4 Inscription) where the chassis is immaculate and you have a Volvo specialist who knows the VEA platform intimately. Rebuilt engines service

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** All replacement engines through our network are supplied with 12‑month warranty and can be fitted by Volvo specialists nationwide. Supply & fit service
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The D4204T14 sits across a value range - from £3,000 V40 D4s to £20,000 XC90 D4s. For a sub‑£4,000 car, a reconditioned engine at £2,500-£3,800 may represent 70‑100% of the car's value - evaluate scrap value before committing. For XC60, XC90, S90 and V90 owners, the car's retained value comfortably absorbs a recon engine cost. Be honest about the car's condition, mileage and MOT history before deciding.

items.question: What is the common failure on the D4204T14 engine?
items.answer: The D4204T14 benefits from improved EGR cooling over earlier variants, but carbon buildup in the EGR valve and intake system can still occur at higher mileages (80,000-120,000 miles). Secondary issues include PCV system clogging leading to oil consumption, and timing belt wear on an interference engine - failure is catastrophic if the belt snaps. The D4204T14 is not subject to the 2019 recall that affected D4204T8, but regular EGR cleaning and strict timing belt adherence are still essential. EGR cleaning recommended every 80,000 miles. Timing belt interval: 93,000 miles or 10 years - failure = full engine replacement. PCV system service at 80,000-100,000 miles.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned D4204T14 engine?
items.answer: It depends on your car's value and the service history of the donor engine. For a V40 or S60 valued under £4,000, a used unit with documented EGR and timing belt history (£1,200-£2,500) may be the only financially sensible option. For XC60, XC90, S90 and V90 owners where the car is worth £7,000+, a reconditioned unit (£2,500-£4,200) with a 12‑month warranty and all known issues addressed is almost always the better investment - the D4204T14's sensitivity to EGR and timing maintenance makes a reconditioned unit with known history significantly more reliable. Used: lower cost, higher risk of inheriting EGR/timing issues. Reconditioned: all common failure points addressed, 12‑24 month warranty. For D4204T14: insist on EGR cleaning and timing belt records.

items.question: What's the difference between D4204T5, D4204T8 and D4204T14?
items.answer: These are all VEA 2.0‑litre diesel sub-codes with different power outputs and revisions. D4204T5 is the 181hp D4 (2010-2015) - the most common UK variant and most frequently reported for oil consumption. D4204T8 is the 181hp D4 (2012-2019) that was subject to the EGR/intake manifold fire recall (November 2019). D4204T14 is the later 190hp D4 (2014+) with improved EGR cooling, revised PCV system, and a longer timing belt interval - considered the most reliable of the three. D4204T5: 181hp, early single-turbo, oil consumption risk. D4204T8: 181hp, recall variant - check if recall work done. D4204T14: 190hp, improved EGR, best choice for replacement.
bullets: D4204T5: 181hp, early single-turbo, oil consumption risk
D4204T8: 181hp, recall variant - check if recall work done
D4204T14: 190hp, improved EGR, best choice for replacement

items.question: How long does a D4204T14 engine last?
items.answer: With proper maintenance - particularly regular EGR cleaning, strict adherence to the timing belt interval, and oil changes with the correct 0W‑20 VCC RBS0‑2AE spec - 180,000-220,000 miles is achievable before major work is needed. The D4204T14 is considered the most reliable VEA diesel, with fewer reports of the catastrophic EGR failures that affected earlier variants. Many D4204T14 units in V40s, S60s and XC60s exceed 200,000 miles with the EGR and timing issues addressed proactively. Timing belt interval: 93,000 miles or 10 years - failure is catastrophic. EGR cleaning every 80,000 miles prevents buildup. Regular motorway driving keeps DPF healthy.
